lesson.title: Variable Scope: Where Names Live and Who Can See Them
lesson.summary: A variable's scope is the region of a program where its name is recognized; defining a function creates a brand-new scope each time it runs, separate from the code surrounding it.
lesson.body:
Variable assignment binds a name to a value, but it does not by itself say where that name can be used afterward. That question is answered by scope: the region of a program in which a given name is recognized. Function definition is what introduces new scopes into a program. Every time a function is called, Python creates a fresh, private area to hold the names created inside that call, separate from the names that exist at the top level of the file.

This separation is easiest to see by trying to reach inside a function from the outside. Consider:

def compute_area(radius):
    pi = 3.14159
    return pi * radius ** 2

print(compute_area(2))
print(pi)

The first call works as expected: compute_area(2) creates pi inside its own scope, computes 3.14159 * 2 ** 2, which is 12.56636, and returns it, so print(compute_area(2)) displays 12.56636. But print(pi) on the next line fails with NameError: name 'pi' is not defined. The variable pi was created inside compute_area's scope during that call, and it stops existing the moment the function returns. The surrounding code, outside the function, was never part of that scope and has no way to see into it.

This scoping applies to more than variables a programmer writes explicitly. A function's own parameters, like radius in compute_area, are part of that same local scope: they are created the moment the call begins, populated with whatever argument was passed in, and destroyed when the call ends, exactly like pi. When Python looks up a name, it checks the current local scope first, which is why the function found pi immediately without needing to search anywhere else.

If a name is not found in the local scope, Python does not give up right away; it looks outward, eventually reaching the global scope of the file, and only raises NameError once the name cannot be found anywhere along that path. This outward search is what allows code inside a function to read variables defined outside it, even though, as the pi example showed, the reverse is not true: outside code can never reach inward into a function's local scope.

Each call to a function gets its own independent scope, even calls to the same function one after another, and even recursive calls to itself. Nothing that happens to a name inside one call leaks into another call, unless that name lives outside the function entirely, in which case both calls are looking at the same shared name rather than two private copies.

This single idea, that functions create their own private naming area, splits naturally into two more specific ideas covered next: local variables, which are the names created and used only inside a function's own scope, and global variables, which live at the top level of a file and can be seen from anywhere, including from inside functions. A third piece, the global keyword, becomes necessary once a function needs not just to see a global variable but to actually change it from within its own local scope.
